The blueberry crop mostly takes care of itself. There's the field burning, spot spraying, spraying by air, stringing, raking, pulling string, and haying. All told, that's just about 30 days of labor.

In the spring, we burn half the fields. Those are the fields that were harvested the year before. Those fields are then ignored. We harvest half the acreage per year. The half we will harvest get sprayed to kill invasive plants and that happens maybe three times per year. They get sprayed by air for pest control and that's twice per year. The organic fields, some acreage is devoted to certified organic, do not get sprayed.

Before the harvest, the fields get strung. This means there's thin white string that separates the fields into rows. People will harvest the berries in their row. After the fields are harvested, the string is pulled in, wound up, and we try to save it for the following season.

After that, we put hay down on the fields we harvested. That hay is sits on the fields over the winter, covered in snow. In the spring, we burn them. The hay burns long enough to kill any invasive species of insect and plants. This keeps us from having to spray as much because wikd blueberries are quite prolific in the right growing environment.

Then the cycle begins again. The fields we burned in the spring are not harvested that year. They alternate between years. About 200 acres of my berries get harvested each year. They are actually quite lucrative. Though I spent a pretty penny in them, they are now quite profitable.

You average about 5,000 pounds of berries per acre. Wholesale blueberry prices vary, depending on who you're selling to. The cannery will only pay about $0.75 and other businesses pay about $1.00 per pound. Customers can buy them direct at a blueberry stand on the mountain, and those are $2.00 per pound and $4.50 per pound for organic.

But, the harvest season is just two weeks - maybe just a day or two longer, depending in the crop. It can be a bit shorter, as the yield will fluctuate depending on the season. Last year was a bumper crop and we averaged about 5,400 pounds per acre. It took 17 or 18 days to harvest the crop and another three days to pull the string and hay the fields.

This year, I probably won't be in the fields much at all. I've more pressing matters and it's not as if I'm actually needed up there. I enjoy going up and I rake right alongside the other people. Just because I own the place doesn't mean I sit there and watch. I actually have a field boss and he runs everything. I'm just there to get some good exercise in, enjoy the sun, and help harvest my delicious blueberries.

Each day in the field is pretty much the best day ever! We sometimes see deer, moose, bear, rabbits, and birds of all types. They're horrible berry stealing furry woodland critters, but I don't much mind. They don't eat that many berries and I don't begrudge them their berries.

You can pick your own blueberries and those are just $1.50 per pound. But, truthfully, if you're just picking a few pounds for a pie then I have a no charge policy and anyone local is allowed to just come pick berries. I also don't charge the elderly locals and even drop some berries off at some places in Vienna where I know they were involved in the blueberry business, or their family was, long before I owned the place. I have plenty of berries and it has paid for itself, so now it's pure profit. I don't mind sharing and the older folks like getting fresh berries delivered.
